## **Annual Employee Surveys**

The single most frequently raised theme across the comments concerns OPM’s proposed changes to the annual employee survey, addressed in subpart C (§§ 250.302 and 250.303), and the discontinuation of the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey. Six of the nine comments address this subject in some form (comments 0003, 0004, 0006, 0007, 0008, 0009), reflecting its evident importance to stakeholders.

The Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS) is often conflated with the annual employee survey (AES) requirement set in section 1128 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2004, Public Law 108–136, div. A, tit. XI (5 U.S.C. 7101 note), which requires each agency to conduct an annual survey covering two content areas. That statute directs OPM to prescribe survey questions by regulation, and this final rule modifies those prescribed questions. The FEVS was part of a larger effort by OPM to assess a variety of human capital topics, and OPM incentivized agencies to

participate in the FEVS by including the required AES items. By participating in the FEVS, agencies would meet their required survey obligation.

In 2026, after serious consideration, OPM decided to discontinue the Governmentwide administration of FEVS, as it was felt the survey had become a check-the-box activity and did not yield actionable insights sufficient to justify the cost and burden it imposed. (OPM paused the survey for 2025 to allow agencies to focus on other workforce priorities; _see_ OPM, 2025 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey and Compliance with Recent Executive Orders (Feb. 28, 2025), _https:// www.opm.gov/chcoc/transmittals/2025/ Memo%20on%20FEVS% 20ReportsFINAL.pdf_ (delaying the 2025 survey); OPM, Cancellation of 2025 OPM Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (Aug. 15, 2025), _https:// content.govdelivery.com/accounts/ USOPM/bulletins/3ede04d_ ).

FEVS did not provide enough meaningful assessment as a general purpose, one-size-fits-all instrument, nor did it have enough actionable feedback or make a real impact for employees to be worthwhile. OPM’s reasoning is set out more fully in its survey guidance and public statements. OPM, _Annual Employee Survey Administration Requirements—2026 and Beyond_ (July 9, 2026), _https:// www.opm.gov/chcoc/latest-memos/ annual-employee-surveyadministration-requirements-2026-andbeyond.pdf;_ OPM, _Measure What Matters_ , Secrets of OPM (July 1, 2026), _https://usopm.substack.com/p/measurewhat-matters_ .

As OPM has explained, it believes strongly in well-designed employee engagement surveys—surveys that help managers understand whether the organization is aligned around the right objectives, whether employees understand how their work contributes to those objectives, whether managers hold team members accountable, reward excellence, and develop top performers, and whether employees can report wrongdoing without fear of reprisal. But a single, centrally administered annual instrument is poorly suited to those ends: objectives and priorities shift during the year, a ‘‘one and done’’ survey becomes a checkbox exercise, and organizations as large and managerially distributed as Federal agencies are not served equally well by one Governmentwide ritual. Survey data are actionable only when collected at the right level of detail, reviewed by the managers closest to the work, and used to diagnose and correct real problems— which requires agencies to own their

surveys. The prescribed common questions preserve OPM’s visibility into Governmentwide trends so that systemic challenges can still be identified centrally.

_Core Survey Question Set_

Several organizational comments (0006, 0007, 0008, 0009), along with comment 0003, objected to reducing the number of items from sixteen questions to ten, and several—most pointedly comment 0007 and comment 0008— argued this violates the statutory mandate that the survey address specific topics, including work environment, rewards and recognition, and professional development.

It is OPM’s position that the statute underlying the annual employee survey requires OPM to prescribe common questions ‘‘to allow comparison across agencies’’ and requires that results be made public. It does not require that OPM itself administer every agency’s survey instrument, dictate a single Governmentwide field period, or otherwise control agency-level survey logistics. The final rule preserves the statutorily required mechanism for comparability—a common core of required questions appearing on every agency’s survey—while returning survey administration to the agencies that are closest to their own workforce populations and best positioned to tailor supplemental content to their missions. This is consistent with, not contrary to, the statutory design.

For additional context, the items required in regulation have changed before; in December 2016 the regulation was modified to change the number from 45 to 16 items. This reduction in the number of required items allowed the larger FEVS to adapt and meet new needs. The survey, either the FEVS or the AES items, was never meant to be permanent, but allowed to change as the workforce and workplace needed. While OPM acknowledges there are benefits to being able to trend results over time, there are also benefits to refreshing the content to meet the current needs.

Commenters contended that the proposed survey items do not meet the requirements of the statute regarding content areas that must be addressed (comments 0006, 0007) and that some of the items have some technical faults in their design like unclear wording or response choices (comments 0004, 0007, 0008). OPM respectfully disagrees.

Section 1128(a) requires each agency to conduct an annual survey of its employees—expressly ‘‘including survey questions unique to the agency and questions prescribed under subsection (b)’’—to assess (1) leadership

and management practices that contribute to agency performance and (2) employee satisfaction with leadership policies and practices; the work environment; rewards and recognition for professional accomplishment and personal contributions to achieving organizational mission; opportunity for professional development and growth; and opportunity to contribute to achieving organizational mission.

The content areas Congress enumerated therefore attach to the agency’s survey as a whole, which the statute defines to include the agency’s own questions, and not solely to the subset of items OPM prescribes by regulation. Subsection (b) directs OPM to prescribe questions that should appear on all agency surveys ‘‘in order to allow a comparison across agencies.’’ It does not direct OPM to prescribe a separate item for each content area, to prescribe any particular number of items, or to require that an item use the word ‘‘satisfaction’’ or a satisfaction response scale. Section 250.302(a)(1) preserves each agency’s ability to include questions unique to the agency, and the prescribed items accordingly operate as a floor rather than a ceiling.

The prescribed items nonetheless reach each of the statutory content areas. Leadership and management practices that contribute to agency performance are addressed by items (i), (v), (ix), and (x); leadership policies and practices by items (i), (iv), and (v); the work environment by items (ii) and (viii); rewards and recognition for professional accomplishment and personal contributions to achieving organizational mission by item (iii); opportunity for professional development and growth by item (iv); and opportunity to contribute to achieving organizational mission by items (vi) and (vii). Assessing these conditions through agreement-scaled items is an accepted measurement practice and is consistent with the approach used for the Annual Employee Survey items as administered through the FEVS. An employee’s reported agreement that differences in performance are recognized in a meaningful way, or that a supervisor provides ongoing feedback to help the employee succeed and progress in a career, is a direct measure of that employee’s assessment of the agency in the corresponding content area. OPM does not read the statute to require that a content area be assessed only by an item that recites the statutory phrasing.

As to the technical concerns about item wording and response options, OPM has considered each of them and

concludes that they reflect differences in professional judgment about survey design and item construction rather than defects that would prevent the items from assessing the statutory content areas. Agencies retain discretion to supplement the prescribed items where they determine that additional or differently constructed items would better serve their workforce, and OPM will continue to support agencies through guidance such as the Employee Survey Playbook (OPM, _Employee Survey Playbook: A Guide for Federal Agencies_ (July 2026), _https:// www.opm.gov/chcoc/latest-memos/ employee-survey-playbook.pdf_ ) and OPM’s annual survey administration requirements. OPM, _Annual Employee Survey Administration Requirements— 2026 and Beyond_ (July 9, 2026), _https:// www.opm.gov/chcoc/latest-memos/ annual-employee-surveyadministration-requirements-2026-andbeyond.pdf._ OPM is making no changes to the proposed survey items in this final rule.

## _Survey Methodology, Timing, and Public Disclosure_

Some comments claim that a smaller survey or distributed survey effort would be detrimental, or would lack control and standardization (comments 0003, 0006, 0008). As mentioned, part of the reason the FEVS was discontinued was because its one-size-fits-all approach makes it difficult for agencies to assess their own needs without also doing their own survey in addition to participating in the FEVS.

In fact, it was this need for customization that led three large agencies to discontinue participating in the FEVS altogether in years prior to 2025—National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Securities and Exchange Commission all decided to do their own surveys as the FEVS could not meet their needs. While the FEVS did allow agencies to add their own agencyspecific survey items, the number of those items was limited and had to be asked to the entirety of the agency, which may not be appropriate if only a portion of the agency needed to be addressed.

By returning the responsibility of surveying their employees to the agency and decreasing the total number of survey items required, plus giving options for the methodologies that best suits them, agencies will be able to craft survey items and whole surveys that better serve their specific needs. Using these flexibilities, agencies can continue or even expand on content that the FEVS promoted, such as assessing

employee engagement. OPM will continue to assist agencies by providing guidance and expert advice to meet their obligations, such as the Employee Survey Playbook which provides information and considerations for administering a proper survey.

Comment 0008 objected that revised § 250.303(a) removes the current regulation’s enumerated categories of required public disclosure and permits each agency to determine the specific content of its public release, which the commenter argued could allow selective or incomplete reporting. OPM does not intend, and the final rule does not permit, disclosure that misrepresents survey results. The governing statute requires that the results of the annual survey be made available to the public, and § 250.303(a) carries that command forward: each agency must make the results of its annual survey available to the public and post them on its website, subject only to the narrow national security exception stated in the rule.

OPM will address the content of public releases—including publication of the survey instrument, response rates, and item-level results for the prescribed questions—in implementation guidance, and agencies must submit complete results to OPM and OMB under § 250.303(c), which preserves centralized oversight and enables OPM to publish Governmentwide comparisons. OPM has concluded that this combination of a statutory disclosure floor, annual administration requirements, and centralized reporting better accommodates variation in agency size and structure than a single enumerated list, and OPM therefore declines to retain the prior list in regulatory text.

Comment 0008 also expressed concern that agency-by-agency administration could weaken respondent confidentiality and, with it, employee trust and candor, particularly at small components. OPM agrees that confidentiality is essential to reliable measurement. The Employee Survey Playbook addresses anonymity, confidentiality, minimum reporting thresholds, and data-handling practices, and OPM’s annual administration requirements will continue to set confidentiality expectations for agency surveys. Agencies also remain bound by the Privacy Act of 1974, 5 U.S.C. 552a, in collecting and maintaining survey records. OPM will monitor response rates across agencies and will revisit these safeguards in future administration requirements if participation data indicate an erosion of employee trust.

Comments 0006 and 0009 recommended that OPM publish a bridge or crosswalk analysis relating the prior sixteen prescribed items to the ten items adopted in this final rule, so that agencies can maintain trend analysis across the transition, and comment 0009 further recommended adding a prescribed item measuring perceived pathways into senior executive positions. OPM agrees that measurement continuity has value and will publish a crosswalk discussing the relationship between retiring and incoming items as part of its implementation guidance. OPM declines to add an eleventh prescribed item in this final rule; an agency whose leadership pipeline warrants it may add such an item as an agency-specific question, and OPM will consider leadership-pipeline content in future updates to the prescribed set.

Comment 0008 further objected that OPM guidance issued during this rulemaking directed agencies to implement elements of the proposed framework for the 2026 survey cycle before a final rule took effect. The annual survey obligation rests on each agency by force of section 1128 regardless of who administers the instrument, and OPM’s decision to discontinue centralized administration of the FEVS was a programmatic decision committed to OPM’s discretion; it did not require rulemaking. OPM confirms that agencies remain bound by the survey regulations in effect at the time a survey is administered, and this final rule operates prospectively from its effective date.

## **Conforming Amendments**

As proposed, OPM is making conforming amendments to 5 CFR part 250 as reflected in the regulatory text below. References to the Human Capital Operating Plan (HCOP), Human Capital Reviews (HCR), and HRStat quarterly reviews are replaced or consolidated consistent with this final rule. Crossreferences within part 250 are updated accordingly. Additionally, OPM proposed the revised strategic human capital planning and reporting processes to implement Executive Order 14356, which applies to ‘‘all executive departments and agencies.’’ Although the proposed rule explained the purpose and scope of the proposed revisions in the preamble, OPM did not adjust 5 CFR 250.201, _Coverage and purpose,_ and is now making a conforming edit to align Subpart B with the agencies to which E.O. 14356 applies. The final rule revises § 250.201 to apply to agencies covered by 5 U.S.C. 306(f), which is the

same population of agencies already submitting Annual Staffing Plans to OPM and OMB under E.O. 14356. OPM acknowledges that this revision to § 250.201 was not included in the proposed regulatory text. The revision does not make any operative legal change or impose a new substantive obligation. It simply allows the regulation to reflect the existing requirements of E.O. 143566 and the scope the proposed rule described. OPM therefore finds, pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), that good cause exists to finalize this conforming revision without additional notice and opportunity for comment, which would be unnecessary.

## **Expected Impact of This Rulemaking**

## _A. Statement of Need_

OPM issues this rule pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 1103(a)(5), 1103(c), 1401, and 1402, and, as to subpart C, section 1128 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2004, Public Law 108–136, div. A, tit. XI (5 U.S.C. 7101 note). Three deficiencies warrant action. The Human Capital Operating Plan, Human Capital Reviews, and HRStat quarterly reviews overlap in content and are produced on schedules unsynchronized with the budget and performance cycles under OMB Circular A–11; GAO has designated strategic human capital management a high-risk area since 2001, and the area remains on GAO’s High-Risk List as of 2025. GAO, _High-Risk Series: An Update,_ GAO–01– 263 (Jan. 2, 2001), _https://www.gao.gov/ products/gao-01-263;_ GAO, _High-Risk Series: Heightened Attention Could Save Billions More and Improve Government Efficiency and Effectiveness,_ GAO–25–107743 (Feb. 2025). Chief Human Capital Officers frequently lack the authority that 5 U.S.C. 1401 and 1402 presuppose, and the current regulations supply no means of verification. GAO, _Human Capital: Strategies to Help Agencies Meet Their Missions in an Era of Highly Constrained Resources,_ GAO–14–168, at 10–11 (May 7, 2014), _https:// www.gao.gov/products/gao-14-168._ And the annual survey framework no longer serves its statutory purpose: the statute requires common questions permitting comparison across agencies, not a single Governmentwide instrument, and the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey grew too long and too general to be useful before OPM discontinued it in 2026.

OPM received nine comments, none identifying a basis for withdrawal, but several identifying respects in which the proposed rule addressed these

deficiencies imprecisely. In response, the final rule defines the Annual Staffing Plan as the operational workforce plan for an agency’s strategic human capital strategy rather than a substitute for it (§ 250.202), ties its development to the OMB Circular A–11, Part 6 cycle (§ 250.205(a)(1)), and permits integration of quarterly review into existing reviews under the Government Performance and Results Act Modernization Act of 2010 (§ 250.207). Because comment 0009 correctly observed that the proposed CHCO provision stated an obligation without a means of verifying compliance, OPM adopts in this final rule, in response to that comment, an agency-head certification identifying any gaps in CHCO authority with a remediation timeline (§ 250.206), as a means of verifying compliance with proposed § 250.204(e), which was itself subject to notice and comment, and requires coordination with the Chief Financial Officer, Chief Operating Officer, and senior leadership (§ 250.205), while leaving agencies discretion over internal structure.

Comments further warned that the proposed Strategic Hiring Committee and the proposed removal of diversity references could themselves conflict with merit system principles. The final rule confirms that the Committee’s oversight of agency hiring is a governance and workforce-planning function, that the final rule confers no examining, rating, or certification authority on the Committee, and that its members remain subject to 5 U.S.C. 2301 and 2302 in connection with any personnel action they recommend or approve (§ 250.204(f)). The final rule also adopts, as proposed, the removal of nonstatutory references to a ‘‘diverse’’ workforce in § 250.203 and confirms that the removal does not disturb the statutory obligations that remain, including the merit system principle at 5 U.S.C. 2301(b)(1). As to political-tocareer conversions, OPM declines to restate in part 250 obligations already imposed through OPM’s existing preappointment review, and declines, as outside the scope of this rulemaking, the recommendation to prescribe Governmentwide consent and justification procedures for details and reassignments. OPM concludes that the deficiencies identified above warrant regulatory action and that the final rule addresses them while preserving merit system protections and agency flexibility.

## _B. Impact_

The final rule consolidates duplicative human capital planning and

review requirements, reducing compliance burden on agency HR staff. The consolidation of the HCOP, HCR, and HRStat quarterly review into the Annual Staffing Plan, Annual Staffing Review, and Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Review framework is intended to free CHCO offices to focus on substantive workforce management rather than compliance paperwork, as the Senior Executives Association recommended.

The strengthening of CHCO authority, including the new certification requirement, is expected to improve the visibility and effectiveness of agency human capital leadership—addressing a persistent gap documented by GAO.

## _C. Costs_

This final rule affects Federal agencies subject to 5 CFR part 250. The consolidation of planning and review requirements is expected to reduce, not increase, ongoing administrative costs relative to the current framework by eliminating duplicative HCOP, HCR, and HRStat reporting. Implementation costs are expected to be modest and largely one-time, consisting of the work required to review and update agency delegations, policies, and procedures to align with the new framework. This rule affects over 80 Federal agencies, ranging from cabinet-level departments to small independent agencies. For purposes of this analysis, OPM assumes that the work will be performed by employees at the GS–14, step 5 level under the 2026 Washington, DC, locality pay table ($163,104 annual locality rate; $78.15 hourly locality rate), and that the total dollar value of labor, including wages, benefits, and overhead, equals 200 percent of the wage rate, for an assumed labor cost of $156.30 per hour. OPM estimates that, in the first year following publication of this final rule, implementation will require an average of 100 hours per agency, resulting in estimated first-year costs of approximately $15,630 per agency and approximately $1,250,400 Governmentwide.

Comment 0009 stated that this estimate likely understates the resources agencies will need, particularly because agencies are implementing this rule during the same period as the Strategic Hiring Committee and Annual Staffing Plan requirements of Executive Order 14356 and the Merit Hiring Plan, and recommended a phased implementation with a transition year and dedicated training resources. OPM has considered that comment and retains its estimate as a reasonable central estimate while acknowledging uncertainty in both directions. Even if first-year

implementation burden were triple OPM’s estimate—300 hours per agency—first-year costs of approximately $46,890 per agency and $3.8 million Governmentwide would remain modest and far below the threshold for a regulatory impact analysis.

OPM has also estimated ongoing costs. Preparing the Annual Staffing Plan, participating in the Annual Staffing Review, and conducting Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews are estimated to require approximately 120 hours per agency per year, or approximately $18,756 per agency and $1,500,480 Governmentwide under the same labor-cost assumptions. Those activities replace, rather than supplement, the Human Capital Operating Plan, Human Capital Review, and HRStat processes they consolidate, which OPM estimates required at least as many staff hours annually; the net ongoing effect is accordingly expected to be a modest reduction in administrative cost. Agencies will also assume responsibility for administering their own annual employee surveys. Those costs will vary with the administration approach each agency selects, are mitigated by OPM-provided guidance, templates, and the Employee Survey Playbook, and are offset by the discontinuation of agency-side coordination of the Governmentwide FEVS and of the centralized administration costs OPM previously incurred.

OPM does not anticipate that the final rule will impose significant new costs on agencies. The primary regulatory burden—Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews—builds on existing quarterly performance review obligations under the GPRA Modernization Act and is expected to reduce duplicative reporting.

## _D. Benefits_

The final rule is expected to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of Federal human capital management by: (1) consolidating and streamlining planning and review requirements and synchronizing them with OMB Circular A–11 budget and performance planning timelines, freeing CHCO offices for substantive workforce management and eliminating duplication across planning, budgeting, and performance management activities; (2) strengthening CHCO institutional authority and accountability with a verifiable compliance mechanism; (3) better positioning agencies through a decentralized survey process to design and administer surveys because they understand their own missions,

structures, workforces, and management challenges, while a common set of required questions preserves the ability to track Governmentwide trends; and (4) aligning Federal human capital planning with Executive branch priorities while preserving the statutory obligations and merit system protections that govern Federal hiring.

These benefits are difficult to quantify with precision, but their potential scale is large relative to the rule’s costs: Federal civilian personnel costs exceed $300 billion annually, so even fractional improvements in time-to-hire, hiring quality, or retention of high performers in mission-critical occupations would yield benefits many times the implementation costs estimated above. The rule’s expected recruitment and morale effects, and OPM’s response to comments predicting harm in those areas, are discussed in the Workforce Recruitment, Retention, and Morale section of this preamble.

## _E. Regulatory Alternatives_

An alternative to this rulemaking is to retain the current HCOP, HCR, and HRStat framework without consolidation. OPM considered this alternative but determined that the existing framework creates duplicative reporting that diverts CHCO office resources from substantive work. Retaining the current framework would also leave workforce planning unsynchronized with the strategic planning and budget formulation cycle under OMB Circular A–11 and with the Annual Staffing Plan process established by Executive Order 14356, forcing agencies to maintain two parallel planning vocabularies and documentation streams for the same activity. Nor has the status quo produced results: strategic human capital management has remained on GAO’s High-Risk List for a quarter century under the existing regulatory architecture. OPM also considered a narrower variation—retaining the Human Capital Operating Plan while adjusting its timing and content requirements—and rejected it for the same reasons: incremental adjustment would preserve the duplication that is the central defect of the current framework.

Another alternative is to continue a centralized survey administration. OPM considered this alternative but determined that a decentralized administration positions agencies better by giving them the flexibility and customizability of administering their own surveys while incorporating the items OPM issues in regulation to ensure comparability across agencies. In

evaluating this alternative, OPM also considered the variant urged by several commenters: retaining centralized administration while shortening the instrument and expanding agencyspecific supplements. That approach would preserve the cost of central administration and a single Governmentwide field period while still denying agencies control over timing, methodology, and level of reporting detail—the limitations that led the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Securities and Exchange Commission to leave the FEVS even before 2025. The final rule instead secures comparability through the common prescribed items and the centralized submission of complete results to OPM and OMB under § 250.303(c), while leaving administration with the agencies where the results must be acted upon. Finally, OPM considered delaying the effective date or phasing the new framework in over multiple years, as comment 0009 recommended. However, OPM determined that a delayed effective date would postpone the benefits of consolidation without materially reducing transition costs, because agencies are already required to prepare Annual Staffing Plans under Executive Order 14356 regardless of when this rule takes effect.

## _F. Severability_

If any provision of this rule is held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstance, it shall be severable from its respective section or sections and shall not affect the remainder thereof or the application of the provision to other persons not similarly situated or to other dissimilar circumstances.

## **Regulatory Compliance**

## _A. Regulatory Flexibility Act_

The Director of OPM certifies that this rulemaking will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it applies only to Federal agencies and employees.

## _B. Regulatory Review_

OPM has examined the impact of this rule as required by Executive Orders 12866 and 13563, which direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public, health, and safety effects, distributive

impacts, and equity). A regulatory impact analysis must be prepared for rules with effects of $100 million or more in any one year. This rulemaking does not reach that threshold but has otherwise been designated as a ‘‘significant regulatory action’’ under section 3(f) of Executive Order 12866. This rule is not considered an Executive Order 14192 regulatory action because it imposes no more than de minimis costs.

## _C. Federalism_

This regulation will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the National Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of Government. Therefore, in accordance with Executive Order 13132, OPM has determined that this rulemaking does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a federalism summary impact statement.

## _D. Civil Justice Reform_

This regulation meets the applicable standards set forth in section 3(a) and (b)(2) of Executive Order 12988.

_E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995_

Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule that would impose spending costs on State, local, or tribal governments in the aggregate, or on the private sector, of $100 million in 1995 dollars in any one year, updated annually for inflation. That threshold is currently approximately $206 million. This rule applies only to Federal agencies and employees and therefore does not impose spending costs on State, local, or Tribal governments or the private sector.

## _F. Congressional Review Act_

The Office of Management and Budget’s Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has determined this rule does not meet the criteria listed in 5 U.S.C. 804(2). In addition, this is a rule relating to agency management or personnel and does not come within the meaning of the term ‘‘rule’’ as used in 5 U.S.C. 804(3)(C). Therefore, the reporting requirement of 5 U.S.C. 801 does not apply.

## _G. Paperwork Reduction Act_

■ 8. Revise § 250.205 to read as follows:

### **§ 250.205 Annual Staffing Plans and quarterly updates.**

(a) Each agency must develop an Annual Staffing Plan that aligns with the Agency Strategic Plan, Annual Performance Plan, Agency Budget, President’s Management Agenda, and the HCF. The plan must identify workforce priorities, hiring goals, and staffing strategies necessary to support mission accomplishment.

(1) The Annual Staffing Plan must be developed on a timeline consistent with the agency’s strategic planning and budget formulation cycle under the Office of Management and Budget Circular A–11, Part 6.

(2) The Chief Human Capital Officer must coordinate the Annual Staffing Plan with their agency’s Chief Financial Officer, Chief Operating Officer, and senior leadership.

(b) Each agency’s Annual Staffing Plan must:

(1) Include metrics, frameworks, and criteria for evaluating the agency’s current and future workforce and staffing needs;

(2) Target the agency’s hiring to address skills gaps, enhance service delivery, enable succession planning, and ensure that new appointments in the upcoming year are in the highestneed areas; and

(3) Include specific plans and goals for improvements regarding the four HCF systems and standards, including measurable performance targets.

(c) Each agency’s Annual Staffing Plan also must consider potential efficiencies that may be derived from organizational restructuring; elimination of unnecessary management layers; elimination of duplicative or nonessential functions and positions;

consolidation of administrative functions; reduction of unnecessary or low-value contractor positions; performance management of employees; internal reassignments; redistribution of workload across positions with similar duties and skill sets; process improvement; and adoption of technology.

### **§ 250.206 Annual Staffing Reviews.**

(a) Each agency must participate in an Annual Staffing Review conducted by OPM and OMB to evaluate implementation of the agency’s Annual Staffing Plan and assess progress toward workforce goals.

### **§ 250.207 Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews.**

The Chief Human Capital Officer must coordinate Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews with the agency Performance Improvement Officer and the Strategic Hiring Committee to evaluate implementation of the agency’s Annual Staffing Plan and assess progress toward workforce goals. Findings from quarterly reviews must be incorporated into the quarterly updates to the agency’s Annual Staffing Plan described in § 250.205(e).
